speaker: John Jumper
title: He won a Nobel here for AlphaFold. Then he left. - John Jumper
question: In drug discovery, why doesn't having accurate 3D protein structures immediately translate into curing complex diseases?
guest: I think the right way to think about this is it's a starting point for biological research. One of the ways scientists really commonly use AlphaFold is they use both experimental techniques and AlphaFold—like taking an incredibly blobby picture with cryo-electron microscopy and fitting an AlphaFold prediction inside it to get both confirmation and atomic detail. The hardest part of drug development is that we do not know how biology works very well. The thing preventing us from curing a complex disease is not that we know one exact protein and if we just had its structure the disease would be cured. It involves the whole body, so we are trying to unravel biology well enough to figure out which proteins interact and how that contributes to phenotypes. Even after you find a mechanism, you still have to figure out how small-molecule drugs stick to a protein and change how it behaves. It's like that old joke about the factory technician who turns one screw a quarter turn and charges ten thousand dollars—fifty cents for turning the screw, and the rest for knowing which screw to turn. We are both learning how to build drugs and learning, in this complex factory of the cell, what we need to do to cure disease.

points.core: Predicted structures serve mainly as starting points paired with experimental validation.
points.note: Accept: combining predictions with low-resolution experimental data like cryo-EM, using predictions to design knockout/mutation experiments, or treating structures as a hypothesis-generation starting point. Do not credit: generic claims that AI cannot replace scientists without explaining how predictions pair with experiments.

points.core: Complex diseases involve poorly understood multi-protein interactions across the whole body.
points.note: Accept: not knowing how biological pathways drive disease phenotypes, system-level biology being the core bottleneck, or complex diseases not reducing to a single protein. Do not credit: vague statements that biology is complicated without linking it to unknown target or pathway mechanisms.

points.core: Knowing which biological target to intervene on differs from designing a binder.
points.note: Accept: distinguishing target selection/identification from small-molecule drug design, or noting that binding a protein does not cure disease without knowing the right biological lever. Do not credit: generic complaints about clinical trial costs or regulatory timelines.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because knowing a protein's shape solves only one early step in a long chain of problems, and usually not the hardest one.

A structure tells you what a target looks like, not whether hitting it will change the disease. Complex diseases such as Alzheimer's, cancer or diabetes arise from networks of many genes, cell types and environmental factors, so choosing the right target is the main bottleneck. Most clinical failures come from lack of efficacy, meaning the biology was wrong, not the structure.

Structures are also static snapshots. Proteins flex, shift between conformations, interact with partners, and some are intrinsically disordered, so a single predicted model can mislead drug design. Even with a good model, predicting how tightly a small molecule binds remains imprecise, and some targets lack usable binding pockets.

Finally, a molecule that binds well is not yet a drug. It must be absorbed, reach the right tissue, survive metabolism, avoid toxicity and off-target effects, and then prove itself in years of human trials, where roughly 90 percent of candidates fail.

Structure prediction speeds up early discovery, but it doesn't remove the biological and clinical uncertainty downstream.

points.why: The response says structure prediction speeds early discovery but gives no role for predicted structures in generating hypotheses or guiding experimental validation.
The response identifies disease-driving biological networks as the reason effective targets are hard to choose.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Knowing a protein’s 3D structure solves only one early step in a long biological and clinical chain. Complex diseases like cancer, Alzheimer’s, and autoimmune disorders rarely stem from a single faulty protein; they arise from intricate, redundant biological networks where modulating one target often triggers compensatory pathways or fails to alter disease progression. Structure alone cannot reveal which targets actually drive human pathology. Moreover, most structural models are static snapshots of isolated proteins, whereas inside living cells proteins constantly flex through transient conformations, rely on intrinsically disordered regions, undergo chemical modifications, and function within shifting multi-protein complexes. Even when a structure reveals a druggable pocket, tight binding does not guarantee the right functional effect or sufficient selectivity to spare closely related proteins. Finally, most drug candidates fail in clinical trials not from poor target binding, but because of whole-body pharmacology: a viable medicine must be absorbed, survive metabolism, cross biological barriers to reach the right tissue at safe concentrations, and avoid unexpected toxicity across genetically diverse patients.

points.why: The response calls structure determination an early step but does not explain how structures generate hypotheses or guide experimental validation.
The response links disease progression to interacting pathways and explains why a protein structure alone cannot identify the drivers of disease.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
A structure tells you what a protein looks like, but not which protein to target, whether hitting it will help, or whether a molecule that binds it will work as a drug. Structure prediction tools like AlphaFold fix one step in a long pipeline.

The hardest step is picking the right target. Complex diseases such as Alzheimer's, most cancers and autoimmune disorders involve networks of genes, cell types and environmental factors. Most clinical failures happen because the target turns out not to drive the disease in humans, not because the molecule failed to bind.

Static structures also leave out a lot. Proteins flex, change shape and form complexes. Many important targets are disordered or have no obvious binding pocket. Predicted models are often not precise enough to estimate binding strength.

Even a molecule that binds well still has to be absorbed, reach the right tissue, avoid off-target toxicity and resist drug resistance. Those properties come from whole-body biology, not from protein shape. Animal models predict human outcomes poorly, so years of clinical trials remain the real bottleneck. Better structures speed up early design but leave most of the risk untouched.

points.why: The response says structures speed up early design without explaining how predictions generate testable hypotheses or are paired with experimental validation.
The response connects the difficulty of identifying a disease-driving target to the interacting biological and environmental factors behind complex diseases.
quotes: The hardest step is picking the right target.
Complex diseases such as Alzheimer's, most cancers and autoimmune disorders involve networks of genes, cell types and environmental factors.

points.why: The response explicitly distinguishes choosing a target whose modulation will help from finding a molecule that binds it.
quotes: A structure tells you what a protein looks like, but not which protein to target, whether hitting it will help, or whether a molecule that binds it will work as a drug.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: An accurate 3D protein structure is only a static snapshot of a single component, whereas complex diseases unfold inside dynamic, interconnected living systems. First, knowing a protein’s shape does not guarantee that targeting it will actually alter the disease; complex conditions like neurodegeneration or cancer often involve redundant pathways, multiple interacting genes, and feedback loops that compensate when one protein is blocked. Second, proteins in the body are not rigid—they flex, shift conformations, form multi-protein complexes, and carry chemical modifications that a static model may miss, making binding-site prediction difficult. Even when researchers design a molecule that binds a target tightly in a computer model or test tube, turning it into a viable medicine is far harder. The compound must be absorbed, reach the right tissue, resist rapid breakdown, and avoid off-target toxicity across the whole organism. Ultimately, most drugs fail in clinical trials because of unexpected safety issues or lack of real-world efficacy in human biology, bottlenecks that structural data alone cannot solve.

points.why: The response describes limitations of static structures but gives no role for predictions in generating hypotheses or guiding experiments.
The response identifies pathway redundancy and feedback as mechanisms that can prevent a single-protein intervention from changing the disease.
quotes: redundant pathways, multiple interacting genes, and feedback loops that compensate when one protein is blocked

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
An accurate 3D protein structure can show where a drug might bind. It can’t tell you whether changing that protein’s activity will help patients. Complex diseases often involve several interacting pathways, and the mechanisms driving the same diagnosis can differ from one patient to another. Even when a protein is a good target, a single structure captures only one of the shapes it can take in a living cell.

A molecule that binds in the lab still has to reach the right tissue at an effective dose, act selectively enough to avoid unacceptable side effects, and produce a meaningful benefit. Structural information helps researchers design and refine drug candidates. Experiments and clinical trials establish whether those candidates are safe and effective.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
An accurate 3D protein structure can reveal a pocket where a drug might bind. It can’t tell us on its own whether changing that protein’s activity will improve a patient’s health. Complex diseases often involve several interacting pathways. A protein associated with a disease may be a consequence of the illness, and even when it helps drive the disease, other pathways may compensate when it is blocked.

Designing the drug poses a separate challenge. Proteins change shape and interact with other molecules, so a compound that appears to fit a pocket may bind weakly or have little effect in a living cell. A useful drug must also reach the affected tissue at a dose that works without causing unacceptable harm. Structures guide the search, while experiments and clinical trials establish whether a treatment actually helps patients.

points.why: The response treats a potential binding pocket as a lead and gives experiments and trials the role of testing whether treatment helps.
